subject: physics
topicDisplay: Unit 6: Energy and Momentum of Rotating Systems
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} question that tests this idea: "{lo}". Then score my answer the way an AP reader would.
promptWeak: Explain this {board} idea simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake students make: "{lo}".

questions.q: A flywheel with constant rotational inertia turns counterclockwise at 12 rad/s. A motor slows it to a stop and then sets it turning clockwise at 12 rad/s, so that, with counterclockwise taken as positive, its angular velocity changes from +12 rad/s to −12 rad/s. How does the flywheel's final rotational kinetic energy compare with its initial rotational kinetic energy?
options: It is the initial value with a negative sign.
It equals the initial rotational kinetic energy.
It is greater, as ω has changed by 24 rad/s in all.
It is smaller, as energy was used up in stopping it.
optionWhy: A student who gives kinetic energy the sign of the angular velocity picks this. Kinetic energy has no direction and cannot be negative; squaring −12 rad/s gives the same value as squaring +12 rad/s.
K = (1/2)Iω² depends on ω², and (+12 rad/s)² = (−12 rad/s)². Rotational kinetic energy is a scalar with no direction, so reversing the sense of rotation at the same angular speed leaves it unchanged.

A student who finds the change in kinetic energy from the change in angular velocity, (1/2)I(24 rad/s)², picks this. The change in kinetic energy is the difference of the two energies, (1/2)I(12)² − (1/2)I(12)² = 0.

A student who thinks energy was used up in stopping the flywheel picks this. Kinetic energy depends only on the angular speed at the instant: it is (1/2)I(12 rad/s)² at the start and at the end, whatever energy was transferred in between.
questions.explain: K = (1/2)Iω² depends on ω², and (+12 rad/s)² = (−12 rad/s)². Rotational kinetic energy is a scalar with no direction, so reversing the sense of rotation at the same angular speed leaves it unchanged.

questions.q: Two small spheres of equal mass are fixed to a light rod that rotates about a fixed axis through the rod's center, perpendicular to the rod. The rotational kinetic energy of the rod–spheres system is K_0. The spheres are moved to three times their original distances from the axis, and the rod is then set rotating at half its original angular speed. Modeling the spheres as objects, the new rotational kinetic energy equals K_0 multiplied by which factor?
optionWhy: A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass keeps I the same and multiplies K only by (1/2)² = 1/4. Moving the same masses to three times the distance makes I = Σ m r² nine times as great.
Each sphere's contribution m r² becomes m(3r)² = 9mr², so I is multiplied by 9. Halving ω multiplies ω² by 1/4. K = (1/2)Iω² is therefore multiplied by 9 × 1/4 = 2.25.
A student who takes rotational inertia to be proportional to distance multiplies I by 3 and gets 3 × 1/4 = 0.75. The distance in I = mr² is squared, so tripling it multiplies I by 9.
A student who treats kinetic energy as proportional to Iω, like momentum mv, gets 9 × 1/2 = 4.5. Rotational kinetic energy depends on ω², so halving ω divides K by 4, not by 2.
questions.explain: Each sphere's contribution m r² becomes m(3r)² = 9mr², so I is multiplied by 9. Halving ω multiplies ω² by 1/4. K = (1/2)Iω² is therefore multiplied by 9 × 1/4 = 2.25.
questions.working: I = Σ m r²: r → 3r gives I → 9I. ω → ω/2 gives ω² → ω²/4. K = (1/2)Iω² → (9/4)K_0 = 2.25K_0. Errors: I unchanged → 1/4 = 0.25; I ∝ r → 3/4 = 0.75; K ∝ Iω → 9/2 = 4.50.

questions.q: The diagram shows, viewed from above, a light rod that rotates in a horizontal plane about a fixed vertical axle at one end. Two small spheres, each of mass 1.0 kg, are fixed to the rod at the distances from the axle shown. The rod rotates with angular speed 4.0 rad/s. Modeling the spheres as objects, what is the rotational kinetic energy of the rod–spheres system?
optionWhy: A student who uses I = Σ m r without squaring the distances gets (1.0)(0.20) + (1.0)(0.60) = 0.80 and (1/2)(0.80)(4.0)² = 6.4 J. Each distance must be squared: I = Σ m r² = 0.40 kg·m².

A student who places the whole 2.0 kg at the center of mass, 0.40 m from the axle, gets I = (2.0)(0.40)² = 0.32 kg·m² and K ≈ 2.6 J. Because distances are squared, the outer sphere contributes more than the average distance allows for; each sphere must be counted at its own distance.

A student who treats all 2.0 kg as moving with the outer sphere's speed, (4.0)(0.60) = 2.4 m/s, gets (1/2)(2.0)(2.4)² ≈ 5.8 J. The inner sphere is only 0.20 m from the axle and moves at 0.80 m/s, so its kinetic energy is much smaller.

questions.q: A small ball of mass m, attached to a light string, moves in a horizontal circle of radius r about a fixed vertical axis with constant angular speed ω. Modeling the ball as an object, which expression gives the ball's total kinetic energy?
options: K = mr²ω²
K = mr²ω
K = mr²ω²/2
K = mrω²/2
optionWhy: A student who adds (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)mr²ω² to (1/2)mv² = (1/2)m(rω)² picks this. For an object rotating about a fixed axis, both expressions describe the same motion, so adding them counts the kinetic energy twice.
A student who treats kinetic energy like momentum, swapping m for I and v for ω in mv, picks Iω = mr²ω. Its unit is kg·m²/s, not J; kinetic energy is (1/2)Iω², with ω squared.

About the fixed axis the ball has I = mr², so (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)mr²ω². This is the same energy as (1/2)mv² with v = rω: the rotational expression and the translational expression are two ways of calculating the ball's one kinetic energy, which is its total kinetic energy.
A student who uses I = mr, without squaring the radius, picks this. For an object a distance r from the axis, I = mr²; the expression chosen, mrω²/2, does not even have the units of energy.
questions.explain: About the fixed axis the ball has I = mr², so (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)mr²ω². This is the same energy as (1/2)mv² with v = rω: the rotational expression and the translational expression are two ways of calculating the ball's one kinetic energy, which is its total kinetic energy.
questions.working: I = mr² (object at distance r). K = (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)mr²ω² = (1/2)m(rω)² = (1/2)mv². Errors: (1/2)Iω² + (1/2)mv² = mr²ω²; Iω = mr²ω; I = mr → (1/2)mrω².

questions.q: A mechanic pushes on a wrench, exerting a torque of 40 N·m on a rusted bolt, but the bolt does not turn. How much work does the torque exerted by the wrench do on the bolt?
options: 40 J, as work done by a torque equals the torque, 40 N·m.
A positive amount, as the wrench exerts a large torque on the bolt.
None, as the bolt turns through no angle as the torque acts.
It depends on how long the mechanic keeps pushing on the wrench.
optionWhy: A student who reads the torque as an amount of work, because both can be written with N·m, picks this. Torque and work are different quantities: work also needs an angular displacement, W = τΔθ, and here Δθ = 0.
A student who equates exerting a torque with doing work picks this. Effort is not work: the torque transfers energy only while the bolt turns through an angle, and the bolt does not turn.

A torque transfers energy only if it is exerted over an angular displacement: W = τΔθ = (40 N·m)(0 rad) = 0. However hard the mechanic pushes, no energy is transferred to the bolt while it does not turn.
A student who treats work like impulse, which depends on how long a force acts, picks this. Work depends on the angle turned, W = τΔθ, which is zero here however long the push lasts.
questions.explain: A torque transfers energy only if it is exerted over an angular displacement: W = τΔθ = (40 N·m)(0 rad) = 0. However hard the mechanic pushes, no energy is transferred to the bolt while it does not turn.

questions.q: The diagram shows a wheel turning counterclockwise on a fixed axle while a brake pad presses on its rim. At point P the pad exerts two forces on the wheel: a normal force F_N, directed toward the axle, and a friction force F_f, tangent to the rim. How does the torque exerted on the wheel by the brake pad affect the wheel's energy while the wheel turns?
options: It transfers energy into the wheel, as it is exerted while the wheel turns.
It transfers no energy, as the wheel's center of mass does not move.
It transfers no energy, as the friction force is perpendicular to the radius.
It transfers energy out of the wheel, as it opposes the rotation.
optionWhy: A student who thinks any torque exerted during a rotation puts energy in picks this. The sign of the work depends on the sense of the torque: F_f's torque is clockwise while the wheel turns counterclockwise, so it does negative work.

A student who thinks work needs the center of mass to move picks this. The wheel turns through an angle, and a torque exerted over an angular displacement does work, W = τΔθ, even though the axle stays put.

A student who applies 'perpendicular forces do no work' to the radius picks this. A force does no work if it is perpendicular to the DISPLACEMENT of its point of application; the rim at P moves tangentially, parallel to F_f, so F_f does work (negative work, as it opposes the motion).

F_N points along the line to the axle, so it exerts no torque. F_f is tangent to the rim and points down at P, where the counterclockwise-turning rim is moving up; its torque is clockwise, opposite to the rotation. A torque exerted against the angular displacement does negative work, so energy is transferred out of the wheel, which slows down.
questions.explain: F_N points along the line to the axle, so it exerts no torque. F_f is tangent to the rim and points down at P, where the counterclockwise-turning rim is moving up; its torque is clockwise, opposite to the rotation. A torque exerted against the angular displacement does negative work, so energy is transferred out of the wheel, which slows down.

questions.q: A light rope wrapped around a large drum of radius 0.80 m is pulled with a constant tension of 1.5 N, tangent to the drum. Friction in the drum's axle exerts an opposing torque, so the drum turns at constant angular velocity. How much work does the rope's force do on the drum while the drum turns through 1.0 revolution?
optionWhy: A student who uses 1.0 revolution as if it were 1.0 rad gets (1.2 N·m)(1.0) = 1.2 J. W = τΔθ needs the angle in radians: 1.0 rev = 2π rad ≈ 6.28 rad.

τ = rF = (0.80 m)(1.5 N) = 1.2 N·m. Δθ = 1.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 6.28 rad. W = τΔθ = (1.2 N·m)(6.28 rad) ≈ 7.5 J. (Check: the rope moves 2π(0.80 m) = 5.0 m, and (1.5 N)(5.0 m) ≈ 7.5 J.) The friction torque does about −7.5 J, so the net work, and the change in kinetic energy, is zero.
A student who uses the tension, 1.5 N, as the torque gets (1.5)(6.28) ≈ 9.4 J. The torque is the force times the radius at which it is exerted: τ = (0.80 m)(1.5 N) = 1.2 N·m.

A student who reasons that constant angular velocity means no work is done picks this. Constant angular velocity means the NET work is zero: the rope's torque does +7.5 J while the friction torque does −7.5 J. The rope's force on its own does positive work.
questions.explain: τ = rF = (0.80 m)(1.5 N) = 1.2 N·m. Δθ = 1.0 rev × 2π rad/rev = 6.28 rad. W = τΔθ = (1.2 N·m)(6.28 rad) ≈ 7.5 J. (Check: the rope moves 2π(0.80 m) = 5.0 m, and (1.5 N)(5.0 m) ≈ 7.5 J.) The friction torque does about −7.5 J, so the net work, and the change in kinetic energy, is zero.

questions.q: A string is wrapped around the rim of a flywheel of radius R and rotational inertia I that can turn on a fixed axle with negligible friction. Starting from rest, the string is pulled with a constant force of magnitude F, tangent to the rim, while the flywheel turns through an angle Δθ. Which expression gives the flywheel's final angular speed?
options: √(2FRΔθ/I)
2FRΔθ/I
FRΔθ/I
optionWhy: The string's torque is τ = RF, and it does work W = τΔθ = FRΔθ. With no friction this is the only torque that does work, so it equals the gain in rotational kinetic energy: FRΔθ = (1/2)Iω². Solving, ω = √(2FRΔθ/I).

A student who takes the work done by the string's torque to be the torque itself, FR, because both can be written in newton-meters, picks this. Work also needs the angle turned through: W = τΔθ = FRΔθ, so the final angular speed depends on Δθ as well.
A student who writes the kinetic energy as (1/2)Iω, without the square, picks this. Rotational kinetic energy is (1/2)Iω², so solving for ω needs a square root.

A student who treats τΔθ like an impulse and sets it equal to Iω, the rotational version of mv, picks this. τΔθ is work and equals the gain in kinetic energy, (1/2)Iω², so solving for ω needs the ½ and a square root.
questions.explain: The string's torque is τ = RF, and it does work W = τΔθ = FRΔθ. With no friction this is the only torque that does work, so it equals the gain in rotational kinetic energy: FRΔθ = (1/2)Iω². Solving, ω = √(2FRΔθ/I).
questions.working: τ = FR. W = τΔθ = FRΔθ = ΔK = (1/2)Iω² − 0 → ω = √(2FRΔθ/I). Errors: work taken as the torque itself, W = FR → √(2FR/I); K = (1/2)Iω → 2FRΔθ/I; τΔθ = Iω (impulse analogy) → FRΔθ/I.

questions.q: A thin hoop and a uniform solid disk have the same mass and the same radius. Each rotates about an axis through its center, perpendicular to its plane, with the same angular speed ω. How does the angular momentum of the hoop about its axis compare with that of the disk about its axis?
options: They are equal, since the masses and angular speeds are equal.
The hoop's is greater, since its mass is all at the rim.
The disk's is greater, since the disk is solid all the way through.
Both are zero, since neither object's center is moving.
optionWhy: A student who thinks rotational inertia depends only on mass picks this. Rotational inertia also depends on how the mass is distributed: the hoop's mass is farther from the axis, so at the same ω the hoop has more angular momentum.

L = Iω and the angular speeds are equal, so the comparison is decided by rotational inertia. All of the hoop's mass is a distance R from the axis, while much of the disk's mass is closer to it, so the hoop has the greater I and the greater angular momentum.

A student who thinks a solid object is harder to turn than a hollow one of the same mass picks this. The masses are equal; what matters is where the mass is. The disk's mass is on average closer to the axis, so its rotational inertia, and its angular momentum at the same ω, is smaller.

A student who thinks an object spinning in place has no angular momentum picks this. Each object's LINEAR momentum is zero because its center of mass is at rest, but each has angular momentum L = Iω about its axis because it is spinning.
questions.explain: L = Iω and the angular speeds are equal, so the comparison is decided by rotational inertia. All of the hoop's mass is a distance R from the axis, while much of the disk's mass is closer to it, so the hoop has the greater I and the greater angular momentum.

questions.q: During a certain time interval, the net angular impulse delivered to a spinning wheel is zero. Which statement about the wheel must be true?
options: Its angular momentum is the same at the end as at the start.
Its angular momentum at the end of the interval is zero.
No torque was exerted on the wheel at any time in the interval.
Its angular speed fell, as no net angular impulse kept it going.
optionWhy: The change in angular momentum equals the net angular impulse. A net angular impulse of zero means ΔL = 0, so the wheel ends the interval with the same angular momentum it began with, whatever torques acted along the way.

A student who takes the angular impulse to be the final angular momentum picks this. Zero net angular impulse means zero CHANGE: a wheel that was spinning is still spinning at the end with the same angular momentum.
A student who reads 'zero net' as 'nothing acted' picks this. Torques in opposite senses can act, together or one after another, and their angular impulses can add to zero; only the total is zero.

A student who thinks a spinning object needs a net torque to keep turning picks this. With zero net angular impulse the angular momentum does not change, so a rigid wheel keeps the same angular speed.
questions.explain: The change in angular momentum equals the net angular impulse. A net angular impulse of zero means ΔL = 0, so the wheel ends the interval with the same angular momentum it began with, whatever torques acted along the way.

questions.q: A wheel mounted at its center on an axle spins with constant angular velocity. Which statement about the net torque exerted on the wheel is correct?
options: It is not zero, since a net torque is needed to keep the wheel spinning.
It is not zero, since the axle and Earth exert forces on the wheel.
It is zero, since a wheel spinning in place has no angular momentum.
It is zero, since the wheel's angular momentum is not changing.
optionWhy: A student who thinks steady rotation needs a net torque picks this. A net torque changes angular momentum; a wheel with zero net torque keeps spinning at a constant rate. Real wheels slow down only because friction exerts a net torque.

A student who thinks every force on a rotating object exerts a torque picks this. The axle's force and the gravitational force both act at the center, on the axis, so they have zero lever arm and exert no torque about it.

A student who thinks an object spinning in place has no angular momentum picks this. The wheel has angular momentum Iω about its axle; the net torque is zero because that angular momentum is constant, not because it is zero.

τ_net = ΔL/Δt. Constant angular velocity with constant rotational inertia means constant angular momentum, so the net torque is zero. Any torque from a motor or from friction must be balanced by others.
questions.explain: τ_net = ΔL/Δt. Constant angular velocity with constant rotational inertia means constant angular momentum, so the net torque is zero. Any torque from a motor or from friction must be balanced by others.

questions.q: Two identical small balls, each of mass m, are fixed to the ends of a light rod. The rod rotates in a horizontal plane about a fixed vertical axle through its center, with negligible friction, and each ball moves with speed v in a circle of radius r. Which statement about the total angular momentum of the rod–balls system about the axle is correct?
options: The balls move in opposite directions, so their angular momenta cancel.
The system's center of mass stays at rest, so there is no angular momentum.
No net external torque acts on it, so the system's angular momentum is zero.
Each ball has angular momentum mvr in the same sense, so the two add together.
optionWhy: A student who treats angular momentum like linear momentum picks this. The balls' linear momenta do cancel, but angular momentum depends on the sense of rotation about the axle, and both balls turn in the same sense, so their angular momenta add.

A student who judges rotation from the motion of the center of mass picks this. A center of mass at rest means zero total linear momentum only; every part of the system turns in the same sense about the axle, so the angular momentum is 2mvr.

A student who confuses constant with zero picks this. With no net external torque, the angular momentum stays constant; it keeps whatever value it has, here 2mvr, just as an object with no net force keeps its velocity.

The system's total is the sum of its parts' angular momenta about the axle. Both balls go around the axle in the same sense, so each contributes +mvr and the total is 2mvr (the light rod contributes nothing). The opposite directions of their velocities do not matter; their sense of rotation does.
questions.explain: The system's total is the sum of its parts' angular momenta about the axle. Both balls go around the axle in the same sense, so each contributes +mvr and the total is 2mvr (the light rod contributes nothing). The opposite directions of their velocities do not matter; their sense of rotation does.

questions.q: An astronaut floats inside a space station, touching nothing and holding nothing, and rotates slowly about an axis through her center of mass. Air resistance is negligible. Which of the following could change her angular momentum about that axis?
options: Pulling her arms and legs in close to her body
Twisting her torso one way and her legs the other
Pushing sideways on a handrail fixed to the station
Waiting, since spinning slowly dies away when nothing acts
optionWhy: A student who equates angular momentum with angular speed picks this. Pulling her limbs in reduces her rotational inertia, so she spins faster, but Iω stays the same: nothing outside her exerts a torque.

A student who thinks internal torques can change the total picks this. Her muscles exert equal and opposite torques on her torso and her legs, so one part gains exactly the angular momentum the other loses and her total is unchanged.

A change in her angular momentum requires an interaction with her surroundings. Pushing sideways on the handrail makes the handrail push back on her; a force whose line of action does not pass through her center of mass exerts a torque about the axis and changes her angular momentum.

A student who believes a spin runs down by itself picks this. With no external torque her angular momentum stays constant indefinitely; objects on Earth slow down only because friction or air resistance exerts a torque on them.
questions.explain: A change in her angular momentum requires an interaction with her surroundings. Pushing sideways on the handrail makes the handrail push back on her; a force whose line of action does not pass through her center of mass exerts a torque about the axis and changes her angular momentum.

questions.q: A student sits at rest on a stool that can rotate with negligible friction about a vertical axle. She holds a bicycle wheel directly above her head with the wheel's axle vertical and in line with the stool's axle, and with her other hand she sets the wheel spinning. As the wheel starts to spin, she and the stool start to turn slowly in the opposite sense. How does the angular impulse exerted on the wheel by the student compare with the angular impulse exerted on the student by the wheel?
options: The one on the student is larger, as the wheel is spinning much faster.
They are equal in magnitude and opposite in their rotational sense.
The one by the student is larger, as her rotational inertia is larger.
The one on the student is zero, as she alone exerts a torque here.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the faster-spinning object exerts the larger torque picks this: the wheel seems to push back on her harder than she pushes on it. The torques the student and the wheel exert on each other are equal in magnitude and opposite in sense however fast either is turning, so the angular impulses are equal in magnitude; the wheel spins faster only because its rotational inertia is smaller.

The student's hand and the wheel exert torques on each other about the same axis, so by Newton's third law the angular impulses are equal in magnitude and opposite in sense, for every instant of the interaction. The wheel spins faster than the student only because its rotational inertia is smaller.

A student who thinks the object with more rotational inertia exerts the larger torque picks this: she seems to deliver more angular impulse to the wheel than it delivers to her. The torques that the student and the wheel exert on each other are equal and opposite, whatever their rotational inertias, and so are the angular impulses.

A student who thinks the object being turned cannot turn anything back picks this. The wheel exerts a torque on her hand while she exerts one on the wheel, which is exactly why she and the stool start to turn the other way.
questions.explain: The student's hand and the wheel exert torques on each other about the same axis, so by Newton's third law the angular impulses are equal in magnitude and opposite in sense, for every instant of the interaction. The wheel spins faster than the student only because its rotational inertia is smaller.

questions.q: A solid ball is released from rest and rolls without slipping down a ramp fixed to the ground. Air resistance is negligible. Consider the system consisting of the ball and Earth. Which statement about the energy of this system as the ball rolls down is correct?
options: U_g decreases by more than the kinetic energy increases, since friction dissipates energy.
The decrease in U_g equals the increase in the ball's total kinetic energy.
The decrease in U_g equals the increase in the ball's translational kinetic energy.
U_g decreases by less than the kinetic energy increases, since friction adds energy.
optionWhy: A student who thinks every friction force dissipates energy picks this. The ball does not slip, so the friction force is exerted at a point that is instantaneously at rest and dissipates no energy.

Without slipping, the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so the static friction force dissipates no energy, and no external work is done on the ball–Earth system. Its mechanical energy is constant: every joule of U_g lost appears as translational plus rotational kinetic energy.
A student who counts only the motion of the ball's center picks this. The ball also rotates faster as it rolls down, so part of the decrease in U_g becomes rotational kinetic energy.

A student who thinks friction supplies the energy of rotation picks this. Friction's torque makes the ball turn, but friction is exerted at a point at rest and adds no energy; all the kinetic energy comes from the decrease in U_g.
questions.explain: Without slipping, the contact point is instantaneously at rest, so the static friction force dissipates no energy, and no external work is done on the ball–Earth system. Its mechanical energy is constant: every joule of U_g lost appears as translational plus rotational kinetic energy.

questions.q: A bowling ball is launched along a level lane so that at first it slides without rotating. While it slips, its rotation speeds up and its center slows down. Which claim about the ball's total kinetic energy while it slips, with its reasoning, is correct?
options: It decreases, since the ball's surface slides over the lane where kinetic friction acts.
It stays the same, since the kinetic energy lost by translation all becomes rotational.
It increases, since friction does work on the ball to set it spinning.
It stays the same, since friction on a turning ball does not dissipate energy.
optionWhy: The point where kinetic friction is exerted moves relative to the lane, so friction dissipates energy, transforming some of the ball's kinetic energy into thermal energy. The total kinetic energy decreases until the ball rolls without slipping.

A student who thinks friction only moves kinetic energy from translation to rotation picks this. The ball's surface slides over the lane, so kinetic friction also transforms some kinetic energy into thermal energy; the rotational kinetic energy gained is less than the translational kinetic energy lost.

A student who thinks friction supplies the energy of rotation picks this. Friction's torque does speed up the rotation, but friction slows the center more than enough to pay for it, and it dissipates energy as the surfaces slide; the total kinetic energy decreases.

A student who applies the rolling rule without its condition picks this. Friction dissipates no energy only in rolling without slipping, when the contact point is at rest; here the ball slips, so its contact point slides over the lane.
questions.explain: The point where kinetic friction is exerted moves relative to the lane, so friction dissipates energy, transforming some of the ball's kinetic energy into thermal energy. The total kinetic energy decreases until the ball rolls without slipping.

questions.q: A solid sphere of mass M and radius R rolls without slipping along a level floor. Its center of mass moves with speed v, and its rotational inertia about an axis through its center is (2/5)MR². Which expression gives the sphere's total kinetic energy?
options: 0.50Mv²
0.90Mv²
0.20Mv²
0.70Mv²
optionWhy: A student who counts only the motion of the center of mass picks this. That is K_trans alone; the sphere also rotates about its center, which adds K_rot = (1/5)Mv².
A student who takes the rotational kinetic energy to be (2/5)Mv², the fraction in the rotational inertia with no factor ½, gets (1/2 + 2/5)Mv². K_rot = (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)(2/5)MR²(v/R)² = (1/5)Mv².
A student who treats rolling as rotation only gives just K_rot = (1/5)Mv². The center of the sphere also moves, so K_trans = (1/2)Mv² must be added.

The sphere's kinetic energy is the sum of its translational and rotational kinetic energies. K_trans = (1/2)Mv². With ω = v/R, K_rot = (1/2)(2/5)MR²(v/R)² = (1/5)Mv². The total is (1/2 + 1/5)Mv² = 0.70Mv².
questions.explain: The sphere's kinetic energy is the sum of its translational and rotational kinetic energies. K_trans = (1/2)Mv². With ω = v/R, K_rot = (1/2)(2/5)MR²(v/R)² = (1/5)Mv². The total is (1/2 + 1/5)Mv² = 0.70Mv².
questions.working: K_trans = (1/2)Mv². Rolling without slipping: ω = v/R, so K_rot = (1/2)Iω² = (1/2)(2/5)MR²(v/R)² = (1/5)Mv². K_tot = (1/2)Mv² + (1/5)Mv² = (7/10)Mv² = 0.70Mv².

questions.q: A satellite of mass 500 kg moves in a circular orbit around a planet of mass 6.0 × 10²⁴ kg. The only forces are the gravitational forces between the two objects. Which statement correctly compares the gravitational forces that the planet and the satellite exert on each other, and their effects?
options: The planet exerts the larger force, so the satellite has the larger acceleration.
The satellite is too small to exert any gravitational force on the planet.
The forces are equal in magnitude, so the objects have equal accelerations.
The forces are equal in magnitude, and the planet's acceleration is negligible.
optionWhy: A student who thinks the more massive object exerts the larger force picks this. The two forces have equal magnitudes; the satellite accelerates far more because the same force acts on a far smaller mass.
A student who thinks only massive bodies exert gravitational forces picks this. The satellite attracts the planet with a force equal in magnitude to the planet's force on it.
A student who thinks equal forces give equal motions picks this. The forces are equal, but a = F/m: the planet's mass is about 10²² times larger, so its acceleration is negligible.

The forces are a Newton's third-law pair, so they have equal magnitudes. By a = F/m, the planet's acceleration is smaller than the satellite's by the ratio 500 kg/(6.0 × 10²⁴ kg), about 10⁻²², so the planet's motion is negligible.
questions.explain: The forces are a Newton's third-law pair, so they have equal magnitudes. By a = F/m, the planet's acceleration is smaller than the satellite's by the ratio 500 kg/(6.0 × 10²⁴ kg), about 10⁻²², so the planet's motion is negligible.

questions.q: A satellite moves in a circular orbit around a planet. Only the planet's gravitational force is exerted on the satellite, and the planet's motion is negligible. Which quantity changes as the satellite moves around its orbit?
options: The satellite's momentum, since the direction of its velocity changes.
The satellite's angular momentum, since its direction of motion changes.
The system's gravitational potential energy, since the satellite keeps falling.
The satellite's kinetic energy, since the planet's gravity pulls on it.
optionWhy: In a circular orbit the satellite's speed is constant but the direction of its velocity turns continually, so its momentum mv⃗, a vector, changes. Its kinetic energy and angular momentum and the system's U_g and mechanical energy are all constant.

A student who treats angular momentum as momentum by another name picks this. L = rmv sin θ about the planet's center has r, v and θ = 90° all constant in a circular orbit, so L is constant even though the velocity's direction changes.
A student who thinks an orbiting satellite keeps losing U_g because it is falling picks this. U_g = −GMm/r depends only on the separation, which is constant in a circular orbit.

A student who thinks any force on a moving object changes its speed picks this. The gravitational force is perpendicular to the velocity at every instant, so it does no work and the kinetic energy is constant.
questions.explain: In a circular orbit the satellite's speed is constant but the direction of its velocity turns continually, so its momentum mv⃗, a vector, changes. Its kinetic energy and angular momentum and the system's U_g and mechanical energy are all constant.

questions.q: A probe is launched from the surface of a planet with exactly the escape speed. The planet has no atmosphere, its motion is negligible, and the only force exerted on the probe after launch is the planet's gravitational force. Which statement about the mechanical energy of the probe–planet system is correct?
options: It is zero, and it stays zero at every point of the probe's motion after launch.
It is positive, since the probe needs extra energy to break free of gravity.
It is negative at launch and rises to zero as the probe gets very far away.
It equals the probe's kinetic energy at launch, since U_g is zero at the planet's surface.
optionWhy: Escape speed is defined as the speed that makes the system's mechanical energy zero. Only the internal gravitational force acts, so the mechanical energy stays at that value, zero, throughout the motion.
A student who thinks escape needs positive mechanical energy picks this. Escape speed is the speed that makes K + U_g exactly zero; a positive value would mean a speed greater than the escape speed.
A student who thinks the system gains energy as the probe climbs picks this. With only gravity acting, K + U_g is constant: U_g rises toward zero and K falls by the same amount.

A student who puts the zero of U_g at the planet's surface picks this. For a satellite–planet system U_g is defined to be zero at infinite separation, so at the surface U_g = −GMm/R, which exactly cancels the launch kinetic energy.
questions.explain: Escape speed is defined as the speed that makes the system's mechanical energy zero. Only the internal gravitational force acts, so the mechanical energy stays at that value, zero, throughout the motion.
